title: Three doors guarded (229–234)
hookLine: guard against anger of the body, of the tongue, of the mind
carry: the mind is where anger first knocks

lines: THE FRONT LOCKED, THE SIDE OPEN.
cards: A house has three doors: a front door, a back door, and a side door by the garage. You can lock the front door every night, but if the side door is wide open, anyone can walk in.
Anger is like a visitor who tries every door. Some of us guard our hands well: we'd never hit anyone. But the tongue is wide open.
Or we're careful with words, and the mind is running a whole courtroom drama in the background. Chapter seventeen ends by checking every door in the house.

teach.b: First, a picture of a person nobody could honestly blame: like a coin of gold from the Jambu river, praised even by the gods. The way there: guard three doors.
Verse two thirty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body!" Verse two thirty-two: "Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue!"

And verse two thirty-three: "Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" Each verse has two halves: stop the harm through that door, and use that same door for good. The body that could strike can also help.
The tongue that could wound can also comfort.
Then the chapter's last line, verse two thirty-four: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled."

teach.h: STOP THE HARM; USE THE DOOR WELL.
teach.b: Buddhist teaching calls these the three doors of action: body, speech and mind, in Pali kāya, vacī and mano. Every action, it says, goes out through one of them.
That's why the ten classic wholesome actions are sorted this way: three for the body, four for speech, three for the mind. Notice which comes last.

teach.h: THE MIND IS WHERE IT KNOCKS FIRST.
teach.b: The mind is where anger first knocks, long before the tongue or the hand. Now look back at the week, a house with good doors. Health is the greatest gift.
Keep good company. Love fully, hold loosely. Good deeds greet you.
Other people are but holding the reins. Overcome by giving.

how: Buddhist ethics sorts action into three doors, body, speech and mind, and the ten wholesome courses of action (three of body, four of speech, three of mind) are a common framework for daily reflection and confession.

o: a door, like body, speech or mind
a guard posted at a monastery gate
a lock that keeps anger out for good

games.q: match each door to its Pali name.

s: the verses only ask you to stop harm through each door
each also says to use that same door for good.
the ten wholesome actions are sorted by the three doors
three of body, four of speech, three of mind.
body, tongue, then mind: and the mind is where anger first knocks.

games.q: you'd never hit anyone, and you're careful with words. but in your head you've been arguing with a coworker all morning. which door is open?
games.why: verse 233: "beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" the mind is the door anger tries first.

practice: Check each door in turn, the body first: notice your hands, your shoulders, your jaw, and let anything clenched soften. Then the tongue: if a sharp sentence is waiting behind your teeth, let it rest there, unspoken.
Then the mind: if an argument is running in the background, notice it, and let it quiet down on the out-breath, three doors closed to anger and open to kindness.

wordCard.voice: Dvāra. A door, a gate: verses two thirty-one to two thirty-four say guard against anger of the body, of the tongue and of the mind, and use each for good.

orig.note: Pali: a door or gate — the teaching of the three doors of action (kāya, vacī, mano) uses this word.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind is where anger first knocks. Body, tongue, mind: one house, well kept. That closes the week.
